items.title: Using Joule Work Desktop and Model Context Protocol to access next-gen SAP Ariba solutions
items.author: FlavioFonte
items.text:
Joule Work Desktop 
 Joule Work Desktop (JWD) is SAP's AI-powered desktop assistant for business users, available on both macOS and Windows. It provides a conversational interface to a large language model (LLM) — but unlike a simple chatbot, it goes far beyond Q&A. 
 At its core, JWD is a productivity platform that brings together: 
 Conversational AI — natural language responses with Markdown, code blocks, tables, and structured visuals (cards, KPIs, charts) 
 Local file access — read, write, edit, and search files directly from your computer within a sandboxed, secure folder 
 Terminal execution — run Python, Node.js, and shell scripts from within a conversation 
 Web search — real-time grounding of AI responses with external sources 
 Microsoft 365 integration — email (Outlook), calendar, Teams, To Do, and OneDrive/SharePoint, all accessible via natural language 
 Spaces — persistent dashboards where data-backed cards (KPIs, tables, charts) refresh automatically over time 
 Skills — reusable instruction sets (playbooks) that extend Joule's expertise for specific workflows or domains 
 JWD is designed for the modern knowledge worker who needs to act across tools, data, and systems — without switching context constantly. 
 What is the Model Context Protocol 
 The Model Context Protocol ( MCP ) is an open standard and open-source framework introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 to standardize the way AI systems like Large Language Models (LLMs) integrate and share data with external tools, systems, and data sources. MCP provides a standardized interface for reading files, executing functions, and handling contextual prompts. 
 The benefit of the MCP is clear, instead of maintaining a complex set of integrations yourself, you can leverage MCP servers that handle the heavy lifting of connecting to external services. 
 Before MCP, developers often had to build custom connectors for each data source or tool, resulting in what Anthropic described as an "N×M" data integration problem. 
 MCP follows a Client x Server Architecture and the MCP client abstracts away the complexity of server communication, letting you focus on your application logic while still getting access to powerful external tools and data sources. 
 MCP Connectors: Extending Joule to Any System 
 One of the most powerful architectural features of Joule Work Desktop is its support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) — an open standard that allows Joule to connect to virtually any external system through a Connector . 
 What is MCP in JWD? 
 Connectors in JWD are MCP server integrations . They expose tools — functions the AI can invoke — that let Joule read data from, write data to, and automate workflows in external platforms. Think of them as a bridge between the LLM and your enterprise systems. 
 Each Connector: 
 Connects to an MCP server via a URL 
 Exposes a set of tools (API operations) that Joule can call in natural language 
 Supports multiple authentication methods: no-auth, bearer token, API key, or OAuth 2.0 (with PKCE + Dynamic Client Registration) 
 How to Add a Connector in JWD 
 In Joule Work Desktop, connectors are managed under Extensions → Connectors : 
 Go to the Extensions icon in the left navigation bar 
 Select the Connectors tab 
 Click New → Add Connector , enter the name and MCP server URL 
 Configure authentication if required 
 Activate the connector per conversation using the "Select Connector" button in the input field 
 Organizations can also pre-deploy connectors centrally, so they appear automatically as "Organization-Managed" connectors for all users — no manual setup required. 
 Why MCP Matters for Enterprise AI 
 MCP fundamentally changes what an AI assistant can do in a business context. Rather than being limited to knowledge it was trained on, a Joule conversation with active MCP connectors can: 
 Retrieve live data from enterprise systems at the moment of the conversation 
 Trigger actions (create, update, submit) in those systems based on natural language intent 
 Combine data from multiple systems in a single response or Space card 
 Be extended without code — adding a new system capability means registering a new MCP server URL 
 This makes Joule Work Desktop not just an assistant, but a true AI integration layer for enterprise workflows. 
 Accessing SAP Ariba via JWD + MCP 
 With the SAP Ariba MCP Connector , Joule Work Desktop gains direct access to Ariba procurement data and workflows — surfaced entirely through natural language. 
 The Procurement MCP exposes SAP Ariba Buying capabilities through the Model Context Protocol, giving AI clients direct access to requisition reporting, catalog browsing, and requisition creation. It covers 17 tools across three capability areas: reporting, catalog and requisition creation. 
 Once the Procurement Ariba MCP server is connected in JWD and activated in a conversation, users can ask questions like: 
 “Show me the requisitions created in September 2026” 
 "Show me my open purchase orders" 
 "What invoices are pending approval?" 
 "Find suppliers for a given category" 
 "What is the status of requisition [ID]?" 
 Behind the scenes, Joule invokes the Ariba MCP tools, retrieves live data from the Ariba backend, and presents the results — as a conversational response, a structured table, or even as a persistent Space card that refreshes automatically. 
 In the case of the first prompt example where we asked, “ Show me the requisitions created in September 2026”, we used the SAP Ariba MCP connector that connected with an SAP Ariba environment retrieving not only the list of the PR, but also the Total Spend, Number of Requisitions, etc. (See snippet below). 

 This illustrates how we can easily extend next-gen SAP Ariba solutions in an AI-native experience that meet users where they already work, generating specific combined information needed to run business. 
 In the next blog we’ll talk more about extending next-gen SAP Ariba solutions and creating specific functionalities tailored to the customer’s needs.

items.title: access restriction at result recording for MIC based on a operation workcenter
items.author: kraghavanbindhu
items.text:
Our requirement is to restrict the result recording for particular MIC by particular users. Like production should record only PP MIC and Quality should record only quality results in QE51. Since we segregated the QM and PP MIC to seperate operation in Inspection plan with seperate PP and QM work centers. Then tried using the work center authroization Q_CHAR_PRC . But its not working as stated in the note - 1799300 - No authority check for work center in transaction QE51N - SAP for Me. 

 The auth object for work center will work only if the workcenter has been added to the selection parameter on the initial screen of transaction QE51N. 

 So it would be better to use the exit QEEM0003 and QEEM006 to acheive the requirements. Also the inspection qualitfication function also dont have any control in QE51N. There also enhancement only

items.title: code is being used and cannot be deleted - Message No. Q3221
items.author: kraghavanbindhu
items.text:
If you face this issue while deleting the code check all quality notification, defects, task where these codes are used or not. If there are transactional data then this cant be deleted. 

 Even if you delete this the data will be stored in QPGR table with inactive status 
 Even though we used the workaround to delete the code group using 2281926 - Error Q3221 when deleting QM code - SAP for Me its not deleting the codes from table rather setting inactive field in table QPGR. 

 Also there are feasibility to delete the code from table using the workaround 556218 - Usage indicator of codes cannot be deleted - SAP for Me but its not available for our system S4 Core 109 2025 
 At last in snote 3397012 - Get error message Q3221 "Code *** is being used and cannot be delete" when trying to delete a code in a code group - SAP for Me its stated that "The physical deletion of used codes in the database is not allowed to avoid data inconsistencies in other applications". 
 Better we can change the status to below.

items.title: From Metrics to Business Value: Building a Digital Commerce KPI Maturity Framework
items.author: ManimozhiRathinam
items.text:
Launching an ecommerce platform is only the beginning. To continuously improve digital commerce performance, organizations need a structured approach to measuring platform health, connecting KPIs to business goals, understanding customer behavior, and ultimately demonstrating business value. Every search, product view, cart addition, checkout interaction, and purchase generates data. 
 Are we measuring what really matters to the business? 
 It is recommended to execute a phased maturity path rather than a comprehensive analytics program. The approach outlines four phases: Foundational Monitoring, Business Goal Alignment, Digital Customer Journey Analysis, and Enterprise Analytics.

items.title: Dangerous goods in MRO logistics: what Restricted Items brings to SAP S/4HANA
items.author: Pavel_Rovenskiy
items.text:
"How do I track dangerous goods and hazardous materials information through my supply chain in SAP?" If you work with MRO logistics, you have heard this question. Often the answer involves a custom solution, unique to each SAP customer. SAP Product Compliance offers comprehensive standard capabilities, but many MRO customers need something lighter: a way to capture DG-related information for received items, make it visible to everyone in the process, and run basic checks before shipping. That is what Restricted Items for SAP Field Logistics (SAP S/4HANA) delivers. In this post I introduce the capability, show where it fits, and walk through a quick example. In almost every MRO-related SAP implementation project I have been involved in, dangerous goods handling was on the requirements list. 
 In short 
 Restricted Items is a standard capability in SAP Field Logistics, generally available since SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01. 
 It provides a data model and UI for capturing dangerous goods, hazardous materials, and other restriction information directly in logistics documents. 
 It works with all item types, including free text items, rentals, and third-party items. No material master or substance data is mandatory. 
 The framework includes configurable validation hooks and key user extensibility for clean core developments. 
 Restricted item data is accessible from Field Logistics apps across different roles in the supply chain, so warehouse staff, logistics coordinators, and shipping operators all see the same information. 
 It allows connecting external sources of information or other SAP solutions through an API. 
 It is not a replacement for SAP S/4HANA for Product Compliance, which covers full regulatory compliance management. 
 What is SAP Field Logistics? 

 Field Logistics covers the movement of goods between base and remote plants across asset-intensive industries. 
 Field Logistics is part of the SAP Oil, Gas and Energy solution portfolio, but it applies to any asset-intensive industry that runs MRO operations: oil and gas, mining, utilities, wind power, and others. It is built natively on SAP S/4HANA and shares the same upgrade cycle. The solution adds industry-specific capabilities to core SAP S/4HANA processes, covering supplier items, kits, containers, voyages, receipts, and returns through a set of SAP Fiori apps. 

 Field Logistics covers forward supply processes and returns scenarios across multiple item types. 
 For a full overview, see the SAP Field Logistics documentation or the Discovering SAP Field Logistics course on SAP Learning. 
 Tracking dangerous goods in MRO logistics 
 MRO operations regularly handle items that are dangerous, hazardous, or subject to special handling restrictions. A valve may contain a regulated substance, chemical used for maintenance is classified under the IMDG Code, rental tool requires specific packaging and labeling before it can go on a vessel. 
 The information that needs to travel with these items through the supply chain includes attributes such as the UN number, hazard class, packing group, and shipping name. Warehouse staff, logistics coordinators, and shipping operators all need access to it at all process steps. 
 The challenge is that many of these items are free text or rentals. They have no material master record in the system, so there is no standard place to attach dangerous goods data. Another challenge is that this information must be available for everyone handling these items across different roles and applications. In practice, we see customers creating enhancements, unique per each implementation. Restricted Items in Field Logistics is designed to address all these challenges. 
 What Restricted Items brings to the table 
 Restricted Items gives you a standard set of attributes you can attach to any item in Field Logistics, whether it belongs to a purchase order, a delivery, a work order, or a network order. Once entered, this information is automatically cross-linked between all SAP documents for the item and accessible from every Field Logistics app in the process chain. 

 Restricted Item attributes on a record. 
 Category - high-level restriction type 
 Class and Subclass - hazard or restriction classification 
 Packing Group - packaging requirement level 
 UN Number - United Nations substance identifier 
 Shipping Name - official transport name 
 EmS Code 1, EmS Code 2 - emergency schedules 
 Emergency Action Code - response procedure code 
 These attributes are configurable. You can define your own classes and subclasses to match your organization's categories, whether those follow IMDG, the European Agreement concerning the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Road (ADR), internal safety policies, or something else entirely. 

 Configuration for restricted Item attributes 
 If the standard set of attributes is not enough, you can add custom fields through key user extensibility . 
 Each restricted item record also supports text notes and file attachments, so handling instructions or safety documents can travel with the item. 

 Text notes on a restricted item record. Useful for handling instructions or additional context. 

 File attachments on a restricted item record for safety data sheets, certificates, or other supporting documents. 
 The restricted item information is integrated across Field Logistics apps: Manage Logistics (Supplier Items), Process Receipts, Process Cross-Plant Receipts, Pack Containers, Manage Kits, Manage Voyages, Initiate Returns by Product, Initiate Returns by Order, and Process Returned Items. 
 In every app, a Contains Restricted Item field appears in the list page alongside a Restricted Information icon and label. 

 The Contains Restricted Item field and popover give immediate visibility across all Field Logistics apps. 
 The object page shows a warning when restricted items are present. From either view, you can navigate directly to the full restricted item record. 

 Warning is shown in Field Logistics apps if opened object contains restricted item. 
 The dedicated Manage Restricted Items app provides a central view of all restricted item records with full lifecycle visibility, reference document tracking, notes, attachments, and a change log. 

 The dedicated Manage Restricted Items Fiori app. 
 A quick example: dangerous goods information end to end 

 Restricted item information follows the item through both forward and return flows. 
 Imagine a corrosive chemical arrives at the supply base on a purchase order. Here is how its dangerous goods information travels through the process, entered once, visible to everyone. 

 Receiving at the supply base. The Receiving Specialist opens the purchase order item in Process Receipts and creates a Restricted Item record with the hazard class, UN number, and packing group. From this point on, the dangerous goods data is part of the item. 

 Packing. The Warehouse Clerk opens Pack Containers and immediately sees the DG indicator on the delivery item. Clicking it shows the classification details and links to the full record. After the item is packed, the container itself is flagged, and the clerk is warned when opening it. If implemented, a validation prevents packing incompatible items into the same container. 

 Vessel planning. The Transportation Planner assigns containers to a voyage in Manage Voyages . Containers carrying dangerous goods are clearly marked. A warning appears when the voyage is opened, and validations, if implemented, can block incompatible containers from being assigned together. 

 Receiving at the remote site. When the container arrives, the Remote Warehouse Clerk sees the same dangerous goods information in Process Cross-Plant Receipts . 

 Returns. When the item is sent back, the dangerous goods data stays with it. The Maintenance Technician or Remote Warehouse Clerk initiating and preparing the return sees it. The Transportation Planner managing the return voyage also sees it. And when the item arrives back at the supply base, the Warehouse Clerk receiving it can access the same DG data that was created when the item was received from the supplier. 
 Validations and extensibility 
 Restricted Items is designed as a framework. You can build clean core custom validations that run during logistics operations whenever restricted items are involved. 
 The following table shows a selection of the available validation hooks: 
 Validation hook Application Triggered by 
 Assign Delivery Item to Container/Package Pack Containers Packing delivery action 
 Assign Container to Voyage Pack Containers, Manage Voyages Assign action 
 Dispatch Container Pack Containers Dispatch action 
 Initiate Transport Manage Logistics Initiate Transport action 
 Seal Container Pack Containers Seal action 
 Initiate Returns by Product Initiate Returns by Product Initiate Returns action 
 Receive Items Process Receipts Confirm Receipt action 
 There are 16 validation hooks in total, covering packing, voyaging, dispatching, sealing, returns, and receipt processes. See the Restricted Items documentation for the full list. 
 Each validation hook is configured with a custom ABAP class that implements the validation logic. This means implementing validations requires ABAP development, but because the hooks and class assignment are managed through configuration, the approach stays within clean core principles. 

 Each validation hook maps to a custom ABAP class through configuration. 
 Key user extensibility is available through the Custom Fields app: you can add fields to the Restricted Item business context ( FLOG_RESTRICTEDITEM ) using key user adaptation. 
 Restricted Items also exposes an API for integration. If your organization needs to connect to an external dangerous goods database, another SAP component such as Purchasing or SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM), or a third-party system, the API provides the interface. 
 Restricted Item API documentation 
 Restricted Items fits the clean core approach: you use the standard framework and extend it through supported APIs and key user tools, rather than building custom code on the core. 
 What Restricted Items is not 
 Restricted Items is a lightweight, logistics-focused solution. It is not a replacement for SAP S/4HANA for product compliance. If your organization needs full substance tracking, regulatory content with automated updates, safety data sheet management, dangerous goods classification against multiple regulations, or compliance checks embedded across sales, purchasing, and transportation, SAP S/4HANA for product compliance is the right solution. 
 Get started 
 Restricted Items for Field Logistics is generally available since SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01, with additional capabilities in 2025 FPS02. Restricted Items is part of the SAP Field Logistics licence; check SAP Note 3510169 for any current restrictions or prerequisites. 
 Restricted Items documentation on SAP Help Portal 
 What's New in 2025 FPS01: Restricted Items 
 What's New in 2025 FPS02: Restricted Items enhancements 
 What's New in 2025 FPS02: New Application for Centralized Restricted Item Management 
 Restricted Item API 
 Discovering SAP Field Logistics (SAP Learning) 
 SAP Field Logistics documentation 
 Other blog posts about Field Logistics capabilities that you may find interesting: 
 SAP Field Logistics: Centralized Supplier Item Repository for an Optimized Supply Chain 
 SAP Field Logistics: Next Generation Kitting & Staging for MRO Industries 
 If you have questions or want to share how you plan to use Restricted Items in your Field Logistics implementation, I'd like to hear about it in the comments.

items.title: Import Sales Orders
items.author: S-O
items.text:
Hello Experts! 

 We are using the 'Import Sales Orders' app in SAP S/4HANA Cloud. 

 Our pricing procedure consists of the base price (PPR0) and additional condition types (ZPxx). Master data is configured for each condition type. 

 For business operational adjustments, we want to register debit/credit adjustments for these additional condition types (ZPxx) using the Import Sales Orders app. However, when attempting the import, master data values are automatically proposed, preventing correct processing. Setting a value of '\0' to unused condition types also does not resolve the issue. 

 Could you please confirm if this is the intended standard behavior for the Import Sales Orders app? If so, could you advise on the recommended approach to manually update condition amounts via batch import? 

 Best Regards, 
 Saki

items.title: Interview with Manish Prasad: “Touch Any Growth Lever in India and You’ll Find SAP There”
items.author: Andrea Diederichs
items.text:
Few markets are evolving as rapidly as India right now. Manish Prasad, president and managing director of SAP Indian Subcontinent, oversees a market where 60% of the GDP already touches an SAP system. At the same time, AI investment is accelerating, manufacturing is moving up the national agenda, and India is turning out tech talent at scale. 

 About Manish Prasad 

 With more than two decades in technology and business, Manish Prasad leads SAP across India, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka. He works closely with some of the region’s leading businesses, helping them navigate changing markets and make the most of new technology. 

 A seasoned global leader, Prasad has worked across North America, the Middle East, Asia, and Australia, with experience spanning industries from metals and mining to automotive. Before SAP, he held senior roles at Wipro, Accenture, Dell, and Tata Steel. 

 What makes India so strategically important for SAP right now? 

 Prasad: I would look at it through four pillars. The first is the macro economy. India is one of the fastest-growing major markets, with GDP growth in the 6.5% to 7% range and an economy of about US$4.15 trillion today. The aspiration is to reach somewhere between $6 trillion and $7 trillion by the end of this decade. 

 Agriculture, pharma, and services have traditionally been the main drivers. Now manufacturing is being added in a big way through the government initiative “Make in India.” As the country pivots toward manufacturing, SAP can become the nerve wire in that growth story. 
 How India drives SAP’s AI future 

 Read the feature 

 The second pillar is SAP. We are blessed to have a brand that resonates across the country. Touch any growth lever in this economy, and you’ll find an SAP element there—from national critical infrastructure to the large conglomerates driving growth. We have close to 14,000 customers today, but in the corporate segment alone, we see an addressable market of around 100,000 customers. 

 The third pillar is talent. India graduates 2.55 million STEM students every year, and about 16% of global AI talent comes from India. Customers across the globe understand that India will remain an extremely important supplier of talent. 

 And the fourth pillar is government: the push to improve governance, ease of doing business, policy, infrastructure, and logistics costs. Bring all those pieces together, and that is where India becomes unique. 

 So, India’s growth and SAP’s growth are increasingly connected? 

 Absolutely. About 60% of India’s GDP touches an SAP system in some form, which is why I say India’s growth story is mirroring SAP’s growth story. The momentum is also coming from the Indian consumer. The buying power of the average Indian is increasing rapidly, and about 70%–75% of what India produces is consumed in the country. When you have to serve 1.4 billion people, the economy keeps driving itself. 

 Who are SAP’s customers in India, and what do they need most now? 

 SAP’s customer base in India spans large enterprises, the fast-growing corporate sector, and government. In the enterprise segment, that means working with some of the country’s best-known business groups, including Tata Group, Reliance Industries, and Adani Group. 

 Government customers are focused on sovereignty: they want the benefits of SAP platforms, but they also want data and critical processes kept locally, especially in the context of AI. 

 Enterprise customers, meanwhile, are past the proof-of-concept stage. They understand the value of AI; now they do not want to stop at a few pilots or hackathons. They want us to look at their processes end to end and show how the Autonomous Enterprise can improve their KPIs. Either way, the ask is the same: show us the value, and show us fast. 

 What role does SAP India play in SAP’s global AI ambitions? 

 First, we have extraordinary scale here. Whatever you touch in India involves millions, sometimes billions, of records. If an AI use case can move from proof of concept to full-scale deployment here, it proves the model is resilient and can be replicated globally. 

 Second, we have the talent and partner ecosystem to adapt these technologies quickly and cost-effectively for real customer needs. We have seen this with SAP GROW: it has worked well in India because our people and partners can build the right extensions, make the product relevant for customers, and do it at an optimum price point. The same logic is now applying to AI. 

 And third, our market shows how AI and human talent can grow together. This is not a story about AI replacing people. It is a story about AI complementing talent to create the next level of efficiency and growth. 

 What makes India’s talent base distinctive? 

 There is an absolutely positive mindset. India is a middle-class and lower-middle-class country. Many young people come into employment after growing up with constraints. When they get an opportunity, they do not want to miss it. That creates a competitive mindset and a hunger to do better—for their organizations, their families, and themselves. 

 What SAP provides is the platform: a strong brand, fantastic products, clear leadership, and a market that is expanding in a big way. When those pieces come together, they create real excitement and enthusiasm within our talent. 

 What are your biggest challenges? 

 One challenge is that the ambition often starts at the top. Boards want to move fast on transformation, cloud, AI, and the Autonomous Enterprise, but in large Indian organizations, getting that vision through the system can take time. For SAP, the challenge is to reach the right executive level early and help turn that intent into something the business can actually implement. 

 Then there is the question of reach. India is a huge market, and SAP can only do so much directly. To reach tier-two, tier-three, and tier-four cities, we need partners who understand the industry, the technology, and the customer conversation and who can move with velocity. 

 Data sovereignty has also become a much bigger part of the conversation, especially with AI. Customers want to understand how local we are, how data is governed, and how business continuity is protected. That can slow the pace at which we want to move, but it is understandable. Events from the Russia war to the West Asia crisis to tariffs have made organizations think much more deeply about resilience as they adopt new technology. 

 What do you want SAP India to be known for in three or four years? 

 I would like SAP India to be seen as a market that contributes meaningfully to SAP’s growth. The ambition is for India to contribute 6%–8% of SAP’s growth. We may not be as large as the U.S. or parts of Europe in the near future, but we can become a significant growth engine in our own right. 

 Just as important, India should create references that matter beyond India. When SAP brings major offerings such as the Autonomous Enterprise, SAP GROW, SAP Business Technology Platform, SAP Business Data Cloud, or SAP Business AI to market, we should be able to point to strong customer examples here that other markets can use, learn from, and replicate. We have already seen that with SAP GROW, including customers deploying in 50 days. Because the scale here is so large, a reference from India can become a proof point for SAP globally. 

 What is the best part of your job right now? 

 Representing SAP—and I really mean that. What gets me into the office every day is knowing that while we are helping our customers, those customers are helping move the needle for the nation. SAP is an underlying platform for that growth, and that gives me a real sense of pride, joy, and gratitude. The SAP team in India is making that happen every day, and that is what motivates me personally.

items.title: Smarter Charts in SAP Analytics Cloud: Sorting, Axis Synchronisation, and Custom Axis Titles
items.author: Vivek-Varma
items.text:
Charts sit at the heart of every financial and operational dashboard in SAP Analytics Cloud. The decisions analysts and business leaders make depend not only on the data these charts display, but on how that data is ordered, scaled, and labelled. When a chart presents figures in an arbitrary sequence, forces an unnecessary secondary axis, or generates an axis title so long it gets truncated, the analytical signal gets buried under visual noise. These are not cosmetic problems — they affect the quality and speed of decision-making. 
 Until now, three specific gaps stood out for users working with complex visualisations. The Waterfall Chart, despite being one of the most powerful tools for variance decomposition and financial storytelling, offered no way to reorder its bars — users were locked into the sequence in which data arrived from the model. The Combination of Column and Line Chart forced every measure on the Line Axis onto its own secondary axis even when it shared the same unit and scale as the Column Axis or vice versa, cluttering the chart with an axis that may have mixed scales and units. And across all chart types, axis titles were auto-generated by concatenating measure and dimension names — producing labels too long, too technical, and too difficult to customise for a business audience. 
 With the 2026 Q4 QRC , SAP Analytics Cloud delivers three targeted improvements that address each of these gaps directly: sorting in the Waterfall Chart, per-measure axis synchronisation in the Combination of Column and Line Chart, and custom axis titles across all axis-bearing chart types.

items.text:
How can you group your various actions in RAP under a single button, especially if the actions are quite similar? This article will look at the details of implementing this with ABAP. 
 In this article, we will implement the Factory Actions and apply grouping in the UI to better visualize the options for the user. 
 Introduction 
 Displaying every action as a separa te button can make an application to olb ar feel crowded. Grouping related actions in a dropdown offers a simpler way to present these options under one meaningful label. In this blog , we will bring Approve, Reject and Cancel together under a single Status dropdown in an ABAP RAP application. Using UI annotations, we will define an action group and assign the actions to it, creating a more organised interface while keeping each option accessible . 
 Factory Actions 
 Factory actions in ABAP RAP are used to create new business object instances through custom logic. They can be instance-bound or static: an instance-bound factory action can copy values from an existing record into a new one, while a static factory action can create a record with predefined default values. Typical examples include copying an existing record or creating a new record with prefilled data. 
 Distinction for this example: The Approve, Reject and Cancel definitions shown below are instance-bound non-factory actions, not factory actions. They are declared using action rather than factory action and specify result [1] $self. This blog groups these three existing actions under the Status dropdown; it does not demonstrate creating new records with factory actions. 
 Current Status 
 We had already defined the following actions in the behaviour, but hadn't yet implemented them. The following definitions currently exist and are already displayed in the UI. action ( features : instance ) Approve parameter ZA_APPROVE_PARAM 

result [1] $self{ default function GetDefaultsFor_Appr; } 

event TravelApproved parameter ZI_TRAVEL_EVT; 

validation valid_emp_name on save { field EmployeeName; create; update; } 

action ( features : instance ) Reject result [1] $self; 

action ( features : instance ) cancel result [1] $self; 
 Grouping 
 In this section, we want to group the two factory actions. The user should then find the option to create a record under one item and no longer scattered across several buttons, where other actions might also be visible. @UI.lineItem: [ { importance: #MEDIUM },{ position: 20, type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'Approve', label: 'Approve' },
 { position: 30, type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'Reject', label: 'Reject' }, { position: 40, type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'cancel', label: 'Cancel' } ] 
 To do this, we create a group of type FOR_ACTION_GROUP. We give it a description and an " actionGroupId ". In the UI, the group will then bundle all assigned elements as a dropdown menu. As a final step , we need to assign the " actionGroupId " to the buttons. This adds a new line and two attributes to the UI annotations. @UI.lineItem: [ { importance: #MEDIUM }, { position: 10, type: #FOR_ACTION_GROUP, label: 'Status', actionGroupId: 'GRP1' }, { position: 20, type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'Approve', label: 'Approve', actionGroupId: 'GRP1' }, { position: 30, type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'Reject', label: 'Reject', actionGroupId: 'GRP1' }, { position: 40, type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'cancel', label: 'Cancel', actionGroupId: 'GRP1' } ] 
 Conclusion 
 This example brings Approve, Reject and Canc el together through a Status action-group entry and a shared actionGroupId . The annotation change is only part of the story: the project context, grouping rationale and testing observations explain whether the design served the intended workflow . 

 Grouping related actions in an ABAP RAP application is more than a way to tidy the toolbar: it is a decis ion about how to organise the available operations. This walkthrough shows how an action group and a shared group identifier bring existing options under one dropdown without changing their definitions. The key takeaway is to choose a meaningful group label, group options that belong together, and verify the result against the intended workflow. A cleaner layout is the starting point; a grouping that makes sense to users is the goal .

items.title: How to prorate accrual mid year time profile changes ?
items.author: GouthamVarma
items.text:
Hi Everyone, 
 Our client’s time account calendar year runs from April to March. When an employee changes from Scheme A to Scheme B in June, we expect the time account balances to be prorated based on the duration spent under each scheme. 
 Expected behaviour: 
 · Scheme A: The time account allocation should be prorated from April until the effective date of the time profile change in June. 
 · Scheme B: The time account allocation should be prorated from the effective date of the change in June until the end of the time account calendar year in March, rather than granting the full annual allocation. 
 We would like to understand the possibilities for achieving this requirement in SAP SuccessFactors Time Management. 
 May I know to steps and configuration to achieve this? 
 Thank you for your support.

items.title: How can I list and verify secondary indexes in SAP BTP ABAP Environment trial?
items.author: koichi_kk
items.text:
I am using SAP BTP ABAP Environment 2608 HFC5 trial with Eclipse ADT 3.60. 
 I want to define a unique secondary index on a custom table using: 
 CLIENT, CREATED_BY, EXTERNAL_REQUEST_ID. 
 The Table Index creation wizard is available, but I have not created the index yet. 
 I encountered these limitations: 
 - Open ABAP Development Object rejects "type:INDX" with 
 "Object type INDX is not supported". 
 - Open Others > Index Overview opens only the table's general properties. 
 What is the supported way in this environment to: 
 1. List existing secondary indexes belonging to the table? 
 2. Verify that an activated unique index actually exists in the database with the intended fields? 
 Please distinguish repository definitions from physical database verification.

 Having served as Company Lead for a major legacy-to-SAP migration and Chief of Business Key Users (BKUs), I’ve learned firsthand that no ERP system can succeed without pristine data - clean data is the true bedrock of supply chain execution.

digest.headline: Thin day: Claude Code via MCP in ADT for VS Code, a transport-level clean core precheck idea, and a RAP action-group pattern.
digest.overview:
Seven items were collected and several are abstract-only. The most relevant are an ADT for VS Code 1.2 post on connecting Claude Code to an ABAP system through MCP tools (ref 20), a proposed utility that runs Clean Core ATC checks per transport (ref 11), and a short RAP post on grouping toolbar actions (ref 22). Only the RAP post has concrete annotation detail.

For teaching, the useful material is the RAP annotation pattern and two open questions: how to verify secondary indexes in a BTP ABAP trial (ref 26), and what guardrails an AI agent needs when it edits ABAP objects. Treat the AI and clean core claims as unverified until you read the full posts.

releases.summary: Updated MCP tools for ABAP object read/edit, repository search and runtime feeds, as described in a how-to post. Details are not visible in the abstract.

deep_dives.title: Grouping RAP actions with UI annotations
deep_dives.explanation:
The grouping is purely a UI concern. In the metadata extension or CDS annotations you add one line item of `type: #FOR_ACTION_GROUP` with a label (here 'Status') and an `actionGroupId` (here 'GRP1'). Then you add `actionGroupId: 'GRP1'` to each `#FOR_ACTION` line item that has its `dataAction` and label (Approve, Reject, cancel).

The behaviour definition does not change. The actions stay declared as `action (features: instance) Approve parameter ZA_APPROVE_PARAM result [1] $self` and similar. Because they use `features: instance`, the feature control logic still decides per row whether each entry in the dropdown is enabled.

The source post calls these factory actions in its intro and headings, then says they are instance-bound non-factory actions. Use that as a teaching point. A factory action creates new instances (`factory action`), while these return `$self`. The post shows no action implementation, tests or screenshots, so verify the rendering in Fiori Elements yourself.

deep_dives.title: Repository vs database view of secondary indexes in ABAP Cloud
deep_dives.explanation:
The question in ref 26 separates two checks: what is defined and activated in the repository, and what physically exists in the database. In ADT, the Index creation wizard works. But opening type INDX through Open ABAP Development Object returns 'Object type INDX is not supported', and Others > Index Overview shows only the table's general properties.

The post has no answer, so any approach is unverified. A sensible way to teach it is to separate the questions. First, confirm the index definition is in the activated table or index object. Second, find out which database-level evidence is permitted in a trial tenant, since ABAP Cloud restricts direct database access.

A behavioural check is another option: a unique index should reject a duplicate insert on the key fields. This is an inference, not something stated in the post.

deep_dives.title: MCP in ADT for VS Code: what to expose to an agent
deep_dives.explanation:
The post (ref 20) says ADT for VS Code 1.2 provides MCP tools to read and edit ABAP objects, search the repository and read runtime feeds, with Claude Code CLI as the client. It generates a console class and a Books RAP app with service binding. Only the abstract was available.

For developers the design question is which operations an agent should perform unattended. Reading objects and searching are low risk. Editing, activating and publishing a service binding change the system and need a transport and a human review step.

Treat generated RAP code like any junior contribution: check the behaviour definition, authorization handling and ATC results before release.

interview_questions.question: How do you group several RAP actions into one dropdown in a Fiori Elements list report, and does it affect the behaviour definition?
interview_questions.answer: You add a @UI.lineItem entry of type #FOR_ACTION_GROUP with a label and an actionGroupId. Then you add the same actionGroupId to each #FOR_ACTION line item that references the action through dataAction. The behaviour definition is not changed, because grouping is purely presentation. Enablement is still driven by the action's feature control, for example features: instance, so each entry can be enabled or disabled per row. This is different from a factory action, which creates new instances, whereas instance actions here return $self.

interview_questions.question: A table has a new unique secondary index in a BTP ABAP trial, and ADT shows no index list. How would you separate repository checks from database checks?
interview_questions.answer: First confirm the definition: the index must be in the activated table or index object with the intended fields. That is the repository view. Second, the physical state sits in the HANA catalog, and ABAP Cloud restricts direct database access, so what is possible in a trial is limited. In the source question, Open ABAP Development Object rejects type INDX and Index Overview shows only general table properties. A behavioural test is possible: insert two rows with the same key fields and expect the second to fail. That test shows uniqueness is enforced but not the index's physical structure. State this limit when you report the result.

interview_questions.question: What controls would you put in place before letting an AI agent edit ABAP objects through MCP in ADT?
interview_questions.answer: Separate read operations from write operations. Read and search tools carry little risk. Write, activate and publish operations should happen only in a development system, on a dedicated transport, with a named developer responsible. Generated code goes through peer review and ATC, including Clean Core checks, before release. Restrict the agent's authorizations so it cannot release transports. Log what the agent changed. The source post only describes the capability in its abstract, so these controls are design recommendations, not features of the tool.
